note: status is one of measured / estimated / synthesised / modelled. 'measured' means the number is taken directly from a published measurement or official statistic. 'estimated' means it is derived from published figures under a stated assumption. 'synthesised' means it was generated by us to be consistent with published aggregates and does not correspond to any observation. 'modelled' means it is a parameter of the model, not a property of the world.

datasets.label: Burned area, Indonesia, 2015-2025
datasets.source: KLHK / Kementerian Kehutanan, SiPongi 'Indikasi Luas Kebakaran Hutan dan Lahan', national annual recapitulation
datasets.notes: The official Indonesian series: 2015 2,611,411 ha; 2016 438,363; 2017 165,484; 2018 529,266; 2019 1,649,258; 2020 296,942; 2021 358,867; 2022 204,894; 2023 1,161,192; 2024 376,805; 2025 213,984 (provisional, may be revised). This is 'forest and land fire' area and includes grass and scrub fire outside forest. Independent satellite series disagree: a 2025 Sentinel-2 study puts 2019 at 2.64 Mha against KLHK's 1.65 Mha. We use KLHK throughout for internal consistency.

datasets.label: Burned area, Indonesia, 1997
datasets.source: Tacconi 2003, 'Fires in Indonesia: causes, costs and policy implications', CIFOR Occasional Paper 38
datasets.notes: Tacconi revised the 1997/98 Indonesia-wide figure to 11.7 Mha, up from the earlier 9.7 Mha. Most of the burning ran from August 1997 into April 1998 as one continuous El Nino episode, so the split between calendar years is not well defined. We attribute 9.75 Mha to 1997. Treat this as an order-of-magnitude figure on a different measurement basis from the KLHK series.

datasets.label: Burned area, Indonesia, 1998-2014
datasets.source: Regression on GFED4.1s Equatorial Asia carbon emissions (van der Werf et al. 2017, Earth Syst. Sci. Data 9:697), calibrated against the nine KLHK years 2015-2023
datasets.notes: log(burned Mha) = -3.016 + 0.666 x log(GFED4.1s EQAS Tg C), n=9, R2=0.90, RMSE 0.14 Mha. These are NOT published burned-area figures for those years. GFED's Equatorial Asia region is wider than Indonesia, and the carbon-to-area relationship shifts with the peat/non-peat mix, so individual years can be well off. 1998 is the least reliable: East Kalimantan burned heavily in the first half of the year as the tail of the 1997/98 event, on accounting that is contested.

datasets.label: Burned area, Kalimantan, 2019 and 2022
datasets.source: KLHK per-province burned-area recapitulations, as reported by Kompas and IDN Times Kaltim
datasets.notes: 2019: Kalimantan Tengah 317,749 ha, Kalimantan Selatan 131,454, Kalimantan Barat 127,462, Kalimantan Timur 50,055 - sum 626,720 ha, 38% of the national total. 2022: Kalimantan Barat 21,836, Kalimantan Tengah 1,554, Kalimantan Selatan 429, Kalimantan Timur 373, Kalimantan Utara 370 - sum 24,562 ha, 12% of the national total.

datasets.label: Burned area, Kalimantan, 2015
datasets.source: KLHK per-province figures for Kalimantan Tengah (583,833 ha) and Kalimantan Selatan (196,517 ha)
datasets.notes: LOWER BOUND, not a total. We could not locate the 2015 KLHK figures for Kalimantan Barat, Kalimantan Timur or Kalimantan Utara, so the 0.78 Mha shown is the sum of the two provinces we could source. The true Kalimantan 2015 figure is higher.

datasets.label: Burned area, Kalimantan, all other years
datasets.source: National KLHK or GFED-regression total x an assumed 0.29 Kalimantan share
datasets.notes: The 0.29 share is the mean of the three years where we located KLHK per-province recaps: 2019 (0.38), 2022 (0.12) and 2023 Jan-Aug (0.36). Kalimantan's real share varies a great deal year to year - it is high in El Nino years when the peat domes dry out, and low in La Nina years when Nusa Tenggara grass fires dominate the national figure. A single fixed share is an assumption, not a measurement, and it flattens exactly the variation the model cares about.

datasets.label: Season start / peak / end dates and duration
datasets.source: Derived from ERA5 daily precipitation (Open-Meteo Archive API) averaged over three southern-Kalimantan peat-belt points: Palangka Raya, Banjarmasin, and Kapuas/Sebangau
datasets.notes: These are drought-window dates, NOT observed first-fire and last-fire dates. Rule: start = first day on or after 1 May with 30-day antecedent rainfall below 120 mm (below 180 mm if that is never met); peak = day of minimum 30-day antecedent rainfall; end = first day more than 7 days after the peak with 21-day rainfall above 180 mm. The rule reproduces the documented episodes well (2015: 5 Jul - 13 Nov; 2019: 12 Jul - 15 Oct; 1997: 30 May - 10 Dec) but it is a rainfall rule, so a model calibrated on these durations is partly calibrated on its own input. 2010 and 2022 have no window under either threshold: duration_days is 0 and the dates are null.

datasets.label: Oceanic Nino Index (ONI)
datasets.source: NOAA Climate Prediction Center, ONI based on ERSST v5
datasets.notes: oni_peak_aug_nov is the largest-magnitude value among the four overlapping seasons centred on August to November (JAS, ASO, SON, OND) - the fire-season window, deliberately not the calendar-year mean. Phase is classified off that peak at the standard +/-0.5 thresholds, which is a simplification of NOAA's five-consecutive-seasons definition. The 2026 row is provisional: the Aug-Nov seasons are not yet published, and the phase is inferred from the JJA 2026 value of +1.80.

datasets.label: Fire carbon emissions and CO2e
datasets.source: GFED4.1s, Equatorial Asia region (van der Werf et al. 2017, Earth Syst. Sci. Data 9:697)
datasets.notes: gfed_eqas_carbon_tg and gfed_eqas_peat_carbon_tg are taken directly from the published GFED table. co2e_gt is those carbon figures converted at 44/12, which assumes all emitted carbon is counted as CO2-equivalent. IMPORTANT: GFED's Equatorial Asia region covers Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea and Brunei - it is not Indonesia and it is certainly not Kalimantan. GFED itself flags that estimates from 2017 onward use a different method and are not suitable for trend analysis. Cross-check: GFED gives 399 Tg C for 2015; Huijnen et al. (2016, Sci. Rep. 6:26886) independently estimate 188 +/- 67 Tg C for September-October 2015 alone.

datasets.label: Excess deaths attributable to haze
datasets.source: Koplitz et al. 2016, Environmental Research Letters 11:094023
datasets.notes: 2015: ~100,300 excess deaths across Indonesia (91,600), Malaysia (6,500) and Singapore (2,200). 2006: ~37,600. These are modelled epidemiological estimates from an adjoint chemical-transport model plus concentration-response functions, published and peer-reviewed - not body counts, and they carry wide confidence intervals. Every other year is null because we found no comparable published estimate; a null here means we do not know, not that nobody died.

datasets.label: Economic loss
datasets.source: World Bank, 'The Cost of Fire: An Economic Analysis of Indonesia's 2015 Fire Crisis' (2016) and the Indonesia Economic Quarterly
datasets.notes: 2015: USD 16.1 billion (IDR 221 trillion), about 1.9% of GDP - more than twice the cost of rebuilding Aceh after the 2004 tsunami. 2019: USD 5.2 billion, about 0.5% of GDP. Covers agriculture, forestry, trade, tourism, transport, school closures and health.

datasets.label: Air-quality peaks
datasets.source: National Environment Agency Singapore (3-hour PSI) via published compilations; Hayasaka et al. 2022, J. Air & Waste Manage. Assoc. 72 (Palangka Raya PM2.5)
datasets.notes: Singapore 3-hour PSI peaks: 226 (Sep 1997), 150 (Oct 2006), 401 (Jun 2013), 471 (20 Oct 2015, the all-time record). Palangka Raya Sep-Oct 2015: PM2.5 to about 400 ug/m3 and PM10 to about 800 ug/m3 with visibility under 0.3 km; a separate report puts a Central Kalimantan PSI reading at 1801 on 24 Oct 2015. PSI is an index, not a concentration, and is not interchangeable with ug/m3. pm25_peak_ugm3 is null for every year but 2015 because we found no defensible measured peak.

datasets.label: Share of burned area on peat
datasets.source: KLHK 2015 breakdown
datasets.notes: 2015: 33% of the burned area, 869,754 ha of 2,611,411 ha, was on peat; the remaining 1.74 Mha was mineral soil. Null for every other year. Note that peat's share of EMISSIONS is roughly half again as large as its share of AREA, because peat burns downward: gfed_peat_carbon_fraction is around 0.50 in big years against a 0.33 area share in 2015.

datasets.label: Hotspot counts
datasets.notes: hotspot_count is null for every year. Published hotspot counts are not comparable across years: they depend on the satellite (MODIS vs VIIRS), the confidence filter and the counting window, and the figures in circulation differ by more than an order of magnitude for the same year. We would rather show nothing than show a number that cannot be compared with the one next to it.

datasets.label: Monthly rainfall and temperature normals
datasets.source: ERA5 reanalysis daily 2 m temperature and total precipitation, via the Open-Meteo Archive API, averaged over 1991-2020 at each provincial capital
datasets.notes: ERA5 is a reanalysis - a physical model constrained by observations - rather than a gauge record, but the totals match published station climatologies closely (Palangka Raya 2670 mm here against about 2666 mm published; Pontianak 2876 against 2896). Daily extremes are smoothed. Annual totals run 2,375 mm (Banjarmasin) to 3,260 mm (Tanjung Selor). The southern provinces have a pronounced June-September minimum - Banjarmasin drops to 58 mm in August - while the north is wet year-round. One point cannot represent a province the size of Kalimantan Tengah.

datasets.label: Province boundaries
datasets.source: geoBoundaries gbOpen IDN ADM1 (simplified release), derived from OpenStreetMap
datasets.notes: Real administrative boundaries, licensed ODbL 1.0, (c) OpenStreetMap contributors. Further simplified here with Douglas-Peucker to under 190 coordinate pairs per province so the whole file ships in 21 kB, and offshore islands contributing under 1.5% of a province's area are dropped. The outlines are therefore approximate at the coast: use properties.area_km2 for area, never the geometry.

datasets.label: Province area and population
datasets.source: BPS-Statistics Indonesia
datasets.notes: Land areas in km2 and populations rounded to the nearest thousand. The five provinces sum to 544,150 km2, i.e. 54.4 Mha.

datasets.label: Peatland area per province
datasets.source: BBSDLP / Ritung et al. 2011 Indonesian peatland map, rescaled to the KLHK 2025 Kalimantan total
datasets.notes: The BBSDLP 2011 provincial figures (Kalimantan Tengah 2.7 Mha, Kalimantan Barat 1.8, Kalimantan Selatan 0.6, Kalimantan Timur including what is now Kalimantan Utara 0.9) sum to 6.0 Mha, while KLHK's current headline figure for Kalimantan is 4.5 Mha. We keep the published proportions and rescale them to 4.5 Mha, then split the old Kalimantan Timur figure pro-rata with Kalimantan Utara. The proportions are published; the rescaling and the Kaltim/Kaltara split are ours.

datasets.label: Peat pool areas (intact and drained)
datasets.source: KLHK 2025 Kalimantan peatland extent (4.5 Mha of Indonesia's 13.43 Mha), reported via Mongabay Indonesia; drained extent ~2.7 Mha from the peatland-degradation literature
datasets.notes: The 4.5 Mha total and the 2.7 Mha drained figure are published; the 1.8 Mha 'intact' pool is the arithmetic residual, and 'intact' is generous - much of it is degraded but not drained. Alternative peat maps put Kalimantan at 6.0 Mha (BBSDLP 2011), so this pool could be a third larger.

datasets.label: Primary and secondary forest pool areas
datasets.source: KLHK 2022 land-cover statistics (Kalimantan forest cover 27.4 Mha; national primary 46.4 Mha vs secondary 43.8 Mha)
datasets.notes: Only the 27.4 Mha Kalimantan forest-cover total is measured. We remove an ASSUMED 2.6 Mha of peat-swamp forest to avoid double-counting the peat pools, then split the remainder primary:secondary using the NATIONAL 46.4:43.8 ratio. Kalimantan is far more heavily logged than Papua, so this almost certainly overstates primary forest and understates secondary. Gaveau et al. (Conservation Letters 2019) report 6.04 Mha of old-growth loss across Borneo over 2000-2017, against 55.8 Mha of old-growth island-wide in 1973.

datasets.label: Scrub, grass and abandoned land pool area
datasets.source: Residual
datasets.notes: A balancing figure, not a mapped class: total Kalimantan land (54.4 Mha) minus peat (4.5) minus non-peat forest (24.8) minus an ASSUMED 13.0 Mha of plantation, cropland, settlement and water. It is the least reliable number in the fuel stock, and it is also the pool that matters least, because scrub carries little fuel and regrows within a season - it is not a stock that can be exhausted.

datasets.label: Fuel load per pool (t/ha)
datasets.source: Ballhorn, Siegert, Mason & Limin 2009, PNAS 106:21213 (peat); van der Werf et al. 2017 GFED4s fuel-consumption ranges (forest, scrub)
datasets.notes: Ballhorn et al. measured a mean peat burn depth of 0.33 m over Central Kalimantan for the 2006 event; at a bulk density of about 0.1 g/cm3 that is roughly 330 t/ha consumed per fire. This is the depth one fire removes, NOT the total peat carbon column - a peat dome can burn repeatedly over decades until it is gone. Forest and scrub values are mid-range picks from the GFED4s fuel-consumption ranges rather than Kalimantan-specific measurements.

datasets.label: PM2.5 emission factors (g/kg)
datasets.source: Stockwell et al. 2016 (ACP 16:11711) and 2018 (ACP 18:2585) for Kalimantan peat; Akagi et al. 2011 (ACP 11:4039) for forest and savanna
datasets.notes: Peat 17.3 g/kg is a field measurement from Central Kalimantan during the 2015 El Nino, with a standard deviation of 6.0 and an observed range of 6.0-29.6 g/kg - so plume mass is uncertain by roughly a factor of two either way. Tropical forest 9.1 g/kg and savanna/grassland 7.17 g/kg are the Akagi et al. synthesis values.

datasets.label: Burn susceptibility per pool
datasets.source: Model parameter
datasets.notes: NOT A MEASUREMENT. The relative annual probability that a hectare of a pool burns in a drought year, normalised so drained peat equals 1.0. The ordering (drained peat > scrub > secondary forest > intact peat > primary forest) reflects the literature - drainage canals are reported to raise local fire risk by a factor of about 4.5, and closed-canopy primary forest rarely carries fire except at drought-year edges - but the specific values are tuned, not observed, and the exhaustion model is sensitive to them.

datasets.label: Deforestation and restoration rates
datasets.source: Global Forest Watch / WRI annual tree-cover-loss releases (deforestation); BRGM restoration totals 2016-2024 (restoration)
datasets.notes: GFW put Indonesia's primary-forest loss at about 290,000 ha in 2023 and about 260,000 ha in 2024. We take Kalimantan's share as roughly 40%, giving 0.10 Mha/yr - the share is our assumption. BRGM restored about 1.6 Mha of peatland Indonesia-wide over 2016-2024 (about 0.18 Mha/yr) against a 2 Mha target for 2016-2020; three of its seven priority provinces are in Kalimantan, so we apportion 0.05 Mha/yr. 'Restored' means rewetting and revegetation works completed. It does not mean peat regrown: tropical peat accumulates at roughly 1 mm a year, so a 33 cm burn is about three centuries of accumulation gone.

datasets.label: Per-year fire clusters (map layer)
datasets.source: Synthesised by us from published annual aggregates
datasets.notes: THESE ARE NOT FIRE DETECTIONS. Every point, size, date, duration and FRP value in app/data/fires/ was generated by us. Do not read an individual dot as a real fire - no fire happened at that coordinate on that date. Cluster locations are drawn around named real fire-prone landscapes (the ex-Mega Rice Project blocks and Sebangau/Katingan peat domes in Kalimantan Tengah, the Kapuas delta and Ketapang corridor in Kalimantan Barat, the Barito lowlands in Kalimantan Selatan), sizes from a lognormal, and dates inside that year's rainfall-derived window. Only two things are tied to published statistics: each year's area_ha total reconciles exactly to burned_area_mha_kalimantan in seasons.json, and the split between provinces interpolates between the two located KLHK per-province recaps (2019 El Nino, 2022 La Nina) on that year's peak ONI. Generation is deterministic, seeded on 20260918 + year. For genuine per-fire records, use NASA FIRMS (VIIRS/MODIS active fire) or the MCD64A1 burned-area product.

datasets.label: Downwind receptor cities
datasets.source: BPS-Statistics Indonesia, Department of Statistics Malaysia, Singapore Department of Statistics
datasets.notes: Coordinates, country and population for the twelve cities the dispersion model reports on. Populations are city or district figures for 2023/2024, not metropolitan areas. No PM2.5 values are stored here - concentrations are computed by app.model.dispersion.
